lessons.title: gracias — "thank you," and a whole family of English words

segments.text: You can now introduce yourself. The next exchange is how are you? — but every answer ends the same polite way, so we learn the courtesy word first: gracias.
vowel-a — the clean ah of father, twice.
r-tap — a single flicked r (not the English one, and not yet the rolled rr): the tongue taps once, like the middle of American butter.
ci-th-s — the ci is a soft s in Latin America (GRAH-syahs) and a soft th in most of Spain (GRAH-thyahs). Either is correct — pick one.
gracias is the plural of gracia ("grace, favour"), from Latin grātia — favour freely given. Saying gracias literally offers someone "graces," i.e. good will in return for theirs.
That one Latin root grātia fans out across English — once you see it, you get a fistful of words for free:
grace, gracious, graceful — the direct borrowings.
grateful, gratitude — being full of grātia.
gratis, gratuity — something given as a favour (for free, or a tip).
congratulate — literally "to wish grace together with someone."
Italian grazie, French grâces, Portuguese graças — the whole Romance family kept grātia, even where everyday thanks went elsewhere (French says merci, Portuguese obrigado).
So gracias is not a word to memorize cold: it is grace, made plural and handed to another person.

segments.instruction: "gracias" — GRAH-syahs, one soft tap on the r
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "gracias" — *GRAH-syahs*, one soft tap on the *r*]

segments.instruction: "gracias" then English "grace, grateful, gratitude" — one family
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "gracias" then English "grace, grateful, gratitude" — one family]

segments.text: What everyday English word is gracias the plural of, at the root? (Grace.) So when you thank someone in Spanish, you are literally handing them — what? (Graces / favours.) Next: the little reply that closes the exchange, de nada.

lessons.title: de nada — "you're welcome," or "it was nothing"

segments.text: Someone says gracias. You need the reply that closes the loop: de nada — literally "of nothing." You're waving the favour off as no trouble at all — the same move English makes with "it's nothing" / "no problem."
d-soft — the d in nada is soft, almost the th of this (NAH-thah), not a hard English d. Spanish d between vowels always softens.
vowel-a — three clean ah sounds: deh NAH-thah.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the phrase

segments.text: de = "of / from" (Latin dē) — the same de hiding in English depart, deduct, descend.
nada = "nothing." And this is the beautiful part.

nada comes from Latin (rēs) nāta — "(a thing) born." From nāscī, "to be born," the same root as English native, nature, natal, re-nais-sance (re-birth). Latin speakers said nōn est rēs nāta, "there is not a born thing" — not a single thing that ever came into being — and over centuries the emphatic nāta ("born thing") wore down until the word for 'born thing' became the word for 'nothing' itself.

So the reply de nada literally says "of [a] born-thing" becomes "of nothing at all." French did the identical trick with rien ("nothing") — which is Latin rem, "a thing." Two languages, same move: the word for thing collapses into the word for nothing.
gracias becomes de nada is a fixed adjacency pair: one turn expects the other. Learn them as a unit, the way English glues thank you becomes you're welcome.

segments.instruction: "gracias" … "de nada" — the full exchange, both voices
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "gracias" … "de nada" — the full exchange, both voices]

segments.instruction: "de nada" then English "native, nature, natal" — nada's true family
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "de nada" then English "native, nature, natal" — nada's true family]

segments.text: nada ("nothing") started life as the Latin word for a born — what? (A thing — rēs nāta, a born thing.) What English words share that "born" root? (Native, nature, natal, renaissance.) Next: the verb the whole "how are you?" question turns on — estar.

lessons.title: estar — "to be," the standing kind
lessons.gloss: to be — but the standing kind, straight from Latin stāre

segments.text: To ask how are you? Spanish needs a verb for being. Today just the verb itself and where it came from; how to use it, and its two forms, come next.

st-no-e — Spanish never starts a word with a bare st-; it props it up with an e: es-TAR. (That reflex is why Spanish speakers say e-Spain, e-student — the same e that Latin stāre grew to become estar.)
r-tap — the final r is one soft tap: es-TAR.

estar comes straight from Latin stāre, "to stand." Hold onto that picture: it is the whole reason this verb behaves the way it does. How you are standing at this moment — well, tired, here, there — is a snapshot, not a permanent fact.
That root stā-/sta- is one of the most productive in English. Estar hands you a large family for free:
stay, stand, stance, station, stable, stationary — to stand or stay put.
state, status, statue, estate — a way of standing (your state is how you stand).
constant, circumstance, substance — "standing with / around / under."
So ¿cómo estás? is, at the root, "how are you standing?"

segments.instruction: "estar" — es-TAR, with the little propping e
"estar" then English "stay, state, status, stable" — all standing
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "estar" then English "stay, state, status, stable" — all *standing*]

segments.text: Which Latin verb is estar — "to be" or "to stand"? (To stand — stāre.) Why does Spanish put an e on the front? (It never begins a word with bare st-.) Name two English cousins. (Stay, state, status, stable, estate…) Next: the two forms you will actually ask with.

lessons.title: estás / está — the two forms, and what they are for
lessons.gloss: what estar is for — a current state or location — and the only two forms you need this chapter

segments.text: Estar is "to stand." Now put it to work. Two forms, one job: saying how somebody is right now.
estar — the verb and its Latin "to stand" root.
tú or usted — why usted takes he/she forms.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: state and location use estar

segments.text: Use estar for a current state or a location — the two things that can change without changing what something is:
a state: estoy bien — "I'm well" (today; maybe not tomorrow).
a location: está aquí — "it's here" (for now).

"How are you?" asks about a current state, so it takes estar. Spanish has a second be-verb for identity, and it arrives in its own later lesson; keeping it out of today's drill lets one contrast settle at a time.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the two forms you need

utterances: you're addressing: tú (informal). form: estás. reads as: "you are".
you're addressing: usted (formal). form: está. reads as: "you are".

segments.text: Notice that está is also "he is / she is." That is not a coincidence and not something extra to learn — it is the usted-takes-he/she-forms rule you already met, showing up for the first time in a real verb.

segments.text: What two kinds of thing does estar cover? (Current state and location.) Which form goes with tú, and which with usted? (Estás; está.) Why is está also "he/she is"? (Because usted takes the he/she verb forms.) Next lesson, you finally ask it: ¿cómo está usted?

lessons.title: ¿cómo está usted? — "how are you?"
lessons.gloss: how are you? — assemble the formal question from cómo, estar, and usted

segments.text: Everything you've built this chapter now snaps together into one question. You already met cómo ("how") and the tú / usted choice back in Chapter 3; you just learned estar. Assemble them.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — assembling the phrase

segments.text: ¿Cómo está usted? = "How are you?" (formal) literally: "In what manner are you standing?"
cómo = "how / in what manner".
está = "you are" (the usted/he-she form of estar — state, not identity).
usted = the formal "you".
Note the ¿ — Spanish opens a question with an upside-down mark so you know the melody is coming before you start reading aloud. (We take that mark apart in a dedicated writing lesson.)

segments.instruction: "¿Cómo está usted?" — formal, for a stranger
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "¿Cómo está usted?" — formal, for a stranger]

segments.instruction: the pieces — "cómo + está + usted"

segments.text: Which be-verb does "how are you?" use — ser or estar, and why? (estar — it's about your current state.) What changes between formal and informal? (The next step changes the ending and pronoun.) Next: choosing the register.

lessons.title: ¿cómo está usted? / ¿cómo estás? — choose the register
lessons.gloss: formal and informal how-are-you questions differ in the verb ending and presence of usted

segments.text: You can already ask a stranger ¿Cómo está usted? Now change only the relationship: ask the same question of a friend.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one question, two relationships

utterances: register: formal (stranger, elder, customer). question: ¿Cómo está usted?
register: informal (friend, peer, child). question: ¿Cómo estás?

segments.text: The formal version uses the third-person ending está plus usted. The informal version uses second-person estás and normally omits tú. This is the same relationship contrast you drilled with se llama / te llamas.

segments.instruction: to a doctor you just met — "¿Cómo está usted?"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: to a doctor you just met — "¿Cómo está usted?"]

swap back and forth — "está usted / estás"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: swap back and forth — "está usted / estás"]

segments.text: Ask both versions until the ending swap is automatic.
Which version fits a stranger? (¿Cómo está usted?) Which fits a friend? (¿Cómo estás?) What two things change? (The verb ending and the pronoun.)

lessons.title: regular / más o menos — the honest "so-so"

segments.text: You asked ¿cómo estás? Now you can answer three ways: great, middling, or a wave of the hand. You already have bien ("well," Chapter 1). Today, the middling answers — because nobody is bien every day.
Recall from Chapter 1: bien — "well." Root? (Latin bene, "well" — same as benefit, benevolent.) So estoy bien = "I'm well." Now the answer for when you're not quite bien.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — two answers

segments.text: regular — as an answer to "how are you?", it means "so-so, average, not great." (A famous false-friend trap: it does not mean English "regular / normal / usual" here.) From Latin rēgula, a straight rod a builder used to check a line — the ruler. So regular is "on the rule, on the average line" becomes middling.
That rēgula rod is everywhere in English: rule, ruler, regulate, regular, regiment, and even rail (a straight rod). All the same straight stick.
más o menos — "more or less," the shrug-answer:
más = "more," from Latin magis ("more") — cousin of major, master, maximum.
menos = "less," from Latin minus — the very word English borrowed for minus, minor, minimum, minuscule.
So más o menos is literally "more or less" — the exact phrase, root for root, that English uses for the same shrug.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: a small answer set

segments.text: You now have a scale to answer ¿cómo estás?:

utterances: más o menos means more or less / meh.

segments.instruction: "regular" — reh-goo-LAR, soft tap on both r's
"más o menos" — a little shrug in the voice
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "más o menos" — a little shrug in the voice]

segments.instruction: answer "¿cómo estás?" three ways — bien / regular / más o menos
segments.source: [YOU SAY: answer "¿cómo estás?" three ways — bien / regular / más o menos]

segments.text: As an answer, does regular mean "normal" or "so-so"? (So-so — the false-friend trap.) What straight-rod Latin word is it from, and what English "rod" words share it? (rēgula becomes rule, ruler, regulate, rail.) Next: put the whole exchange together.

lessons.title: y / ¿y tú? — pass the question back
lessons.gloss: and / and you? — a tiny connector that hands the conversation back

segments.text: You can ask how someone is and answer. One tiny connector turns that exchange around so the other person gets a turn too.
Y means and and sounds like Spanish i: ee. It continues Latin et, also “and.” English borrowed that Latin word intact inside et cetera, literally “and the rest.”

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the shortest return question

segments.text: Put y before a person you already know:
¿Y tú? — And you? (informal).
¿Y usted? — And you? (formal).
Nothing else needs repeating. The little question hands the previous topic back to the other person.

segments.instruction: “Bien. ¿Y tú?” to a friend
“Regular. ¿Y usted?” to a stranger
“y” — one clear ee sound

segments.text: What does y mean? (And.) How do you hand a question back to a friend? (¿Y tú?) To a stranger? (¿Y usted?) Which Latin word survives inside English et cetera? (Et, “and.”)

lessons.title: á é í ó ú — the acute accent, and the two jobs it does
lessons.gloss: the acute accent as a visible exception to Spanish's default stress rules

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script — shape and stroke until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: You've been reading accented words since your very first noun — día, cómo, está, más. Time to make that little stroke make sense. Spanish uses one mark to write exceptional stress — the acute accent, ´, leaning right — and it does two jobs in the words you know. Learn the stress job now; the next lesson adds its grammar-label job.

A short stroke rising left-to-right, sitting on top of a vowel: á é í ó ú. (On the í, it replaces the dot.) One clean up-stroke — the opposite lean from the French grave accent à. Spanish never uses grave or circumflex; if it leans the wrong way, it isn't Spanish.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the mark records exceptional stress

segments.text: Spanish stress is regular, so most words need no mark. The default:
word ends in a vowel, -n, or -s becomes stress the second-to-last syllable (ho-la, lla-mo, gus-to).
word ends in any other consonant becomes stress the last syllable (us-ted, re-gu-lar, es-tar).

The accent appears only when a word breaks that rule — it marks the exception. está ends in a vowel, so the rule wants ES-ta; the accent overrides it to es-TÁ. cómo ends in a vowel (rule wants co-MO) but is stressed CÓ-mo, so it gets the mark. The accent is a spoken stress you can see — it never changes the vowel's sound, only which syllable you hit.

segments.instruction: “hola, llamo, gusto” — second-to-last stress
“usted, regular, estar” — final stress
"está, cómo" — the accent overrides the default
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "está, cómo" — the accent overrides the default]

segments.text: How many accent marks does Spanish have, and which way does it lean? (One — the acute, ´, rising left-to-right.) Its two jobs? (Mark irregular stress; the next step covers its look-alike job.) When does a word ending in a vowel, -n, or -s need an accent? (When its stress breaks the second-to-last default.)

lessons.title: el or él? — the accent as a meaning label
lessons.gloss: the acute accent separates the article el from the pronoun él

needs: a pen and something to write on

segments.text: You know el as the article “the.” Add one acute accent and the same two letters do a different job.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one mark, two grammatical jobs

segments.text: The tilde diacrítica separates words that otherwise look alike:

utterances: no accent: el = the. with accent: él = he.

segments.text: The two words are pronounced alike. Here the accent does not move stress; it labels meaning and grammar. Other pairs will arrive only when you know both words, so this lesson asks you to hold one contrast, not memorize a list.

segments.instruction: “el” — the
“él” — he

segments.text: What is the accent's second job? (Separate look-alike words.) Which means “the”? (El, no accent.) Which means “he”? (Él, with the accent.) Does this mark change their stress? (No — it labels the job.)

lessons.title: ñ — the letter that remembers a doubled n
lessons.gloss: the letter eñe — a tiny second n riding on the first

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script — how to write it until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: ñ is the one letter English does not have — and it has the best origin story in the alphabet. That wavy hat (, a tilde) is not decoration. It is a tiny second n, written on top to save space. Once you know that, you know both how to write it and why it sounds as it does.

ñ = the ny in "canyon" or "onion" — one squished sound, tongue flat against the roof of the mouth. English canyon is, in fact, Spanish cañón with the ñ spelled out as ny. Say "onion," freeze on the middle: that is ñ.
Write a normal n, then a small wavy floating above it. Two strokes, one letter.

Careful: ñ is its own letter, not "n with an accent." año ("year") and ano (a rather different word) are completely different words — the tilde is not an optional flourish, it is a distinct letter of the alphabet, with its own slot in the dictionary.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way: the scribe's shortcut

segments.text: That wave is a medieval shorthand. Scribes copying Latin were forever writing double letters, so they saved a stroke: write the letter once, and put a little mark above meaning "…and one more of these." A bar over a vowel meant a dropped n or m (Latin tantum becomes tãtum); a wave over an n meant nn.
Spanish is full of words where a Latin -nn- did exactly this:
Latin annus ("year") becomes anno becomes año. (That same annus gives English annual, anniversary, bi-ennial.)
Latin canna ("reed") becomes caña; Latin domina becomes donna becomes doña.
So the tilde on ñ is a frozen abbreviation — a thousand-year-old note saying "there used to be two n's here." You are writing a scribe's shortcut.

segments.instruction: "año" — AH-nyo, one squished ny; then English "annual"
the doubled-n words — "año, caña, doña"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the doubled-n words — "año, caña, doña"]

segments.text: What is the tilde on ñ, really? (A tiny second n — a scribe's shorthand for a doubled nn.) What Latin word gives año, and what English words share it? (Annus becomes annual, anniversary.) Is ñ a separate letter or an accented n? (A separate letter.) Next: the two everyday words you will be writing it in.

lessons.title: mañana, español — the ñ in the words you are about to need
lessons.gloss: the two ñ words you will meet next — and the second road to ñ, which is not a doubled n at all

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script — the two forms until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: You can write ñ and you can say it. Two of the next words in this book carry it, and both are worth a minute on their own — because neither of them got its ñ from a doubled n.
ñ — the letter, the sound, and the scribe's shorthand.
mañana — "tomorrow," and also "morning." ma-NYA-na: the ñ is in the middle, and it is the stressed syllable.
español — "Spanish." es-pa-NYOL: the ñ is at the end, right before the -ol.

Now the honest footnote. The scribe's doubled nn is one road to ñ, the one you met with año. These two words took a different road: Latin's -ni- before a vowel. Mañana traces back through maneana to māne ("morning" — the root of English matinée); español comes from Hispaniolus, built on Hispania. In both, a ni sequence squeezed together into the same single palatal sound.
So ñ is where two separate Latin sequences ended up — -nn- and -ni-. One letter, one sound, two histories.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "año, mañana, español" — the ñ in three positions]

segments.text: Where does the ñ sit in mañana, and where in español? (Middle; end.) Did those two get their ñ from a doubled n? (No — from Latin -ni- before a vowel, a second road to the same letter.) What was the first road? (-nn-, the scribe's shorthand, as in año.)

lessons.title: ¿ ¡ — the marks that open a question
lessons.gloss: the inverted opening marks — an early cue for question or exclamation intonation

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script — the two opening marks until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: You've been writing them since ¿cómo está usted? Spanish is the one major language that puts an upside-down question or exclamation mark at the start of the sentence, as well as the normal one at the end. It looks exotic; the reason is purely practical.
¿ …? wraps a question: ¿Cómo estás?
¡ …! wraps an exclamation: ¡Hola! ¡Gracias!
The opening mark is just the closing mark flipped 180° — turned upside down and left-right. To write ¿, draw a normal? and rotate it half a turn: the hook ends up at the bottom, the dot on top.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way — the opening mark is an early cue

segments.text: English lets you read most of a sentence before the final? reveals it was a question — fine, because English usually flags a question early with word order ("Are you…", "Do you…"). Spanish often doesn't reorder words: Tienes hambre. ("You're hungry.") and ¿Tienes hambre? ("Are you hungry?") are the same words — only punctuation and the spoken rising tone tell them apart.

So the Spanish Royal Academy, in 1754, made the opening ¿ official: it warns the reader "a question is starting — read this with rising intonation from the very first word." It's a melody cue placed before the melody, the exact same instinct as the written accent marking stress you can't otherwise see. For a language read aloud, it's genuinely useful.

segments.instruction: read "¿Cómo estás?" — start the rising question melody from the very first word, the way the ¿ tells you to
segments.source: [YOU SAY: read "¿Cómo estás?" — start the rising *question* melody from the very first word, the way the ¿ tells you to]

segments.instruction: "¡Hola!" — the ¡ warns you to begin with exclamation energy
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "¡Hola!" — the ¡ warns you to begin with exclamation energy]

segments.text: Why does Spanish open a question with ¿? (Because word order often doesn't change, so the reader needs an early warning to use question intonation.) How do you write it? (A normal? rotated 180°.) Does it always sit at the sentence's start? (The next step places it around a question inside a larger sentence.)

lessons.title: Where does ¿ begin? — bracket the spoken span
lessons.gloss: opening punctuation brackets only the question or exclamation span inside a larger sentence

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — bracket the spoken span and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: You can open a whole question with ¿. Now place that mark inside a larger sentence, exactly where the questioning voice begins.
The opening mark goes where the question begins, even if the sentence started earlier:
Roberto, ¿cómo estás?
The name Roberto is outside the question. The marks bracket the words that need question intonation. The same principle works for an exclamation:
Roberto, ¡buenos días!
This is why the opening mark is more than decoration. It tells the reader exactly where to begin and end a change in spoken melody.

segments.instruction: “María, ¿cómo estás?”
“María, ¡buenos días!”
begin the new melody at ¿ or ¡, not at the first capital

segments.text: In Roberto, ¿cómo estás?, is Roberto inside the question? (No.) Where does the inverted mark go? (At the start of the question or exclamation span.) What does that placement tell a reader? (Where to change the spoken melody.)

lessons.title: Practice — "how are you?", start to finish
lessons.gloss: the full "how are you?" exchange, formal and informal

segments.text: No new words. This chapter's atoms — gracias, de nada, estar, ¿cómo está?, regular — now assemble into a real exchange, run formally and informally until the register swap is automatic. It picks up right where the Chapter 3 introduction left off.
Formal (a stranger, an elder, a customer):
— Buenos días. ¿Cómo está usted? — Bien, gracias. ¿Y usted? — Más o menos. — [reply to a thanks, later in the chat] De nada.
Informal (a friend, a peer) — only the verb + pronoun change:
— ¡Hola! ¿Cómo estás? — Regular. ¿Y tú? — Bien, gracias.
The glue pattern you just secured is ¿y usted? / ¿y tú? — “and you?” It bounces the question back without repeating the whole sentence.
gracias — thank you ( from grātia, "grace").
de nada — you're welcome ( from "of a born-thing" becomes "of nothing").
estar — the state/location be-verb ( from stāre, “to stand”).
¿cómo está usted? / ¿cómo estás? — how are you, formal / informal.
bien / regular / más o menos — well / so-so / more-or-less.

segments.text: Run the formal exchange, greeting to answer, without stopping.

Which be-verb carries "how are you?" and why? (estar — current state.) Two words swap between formal and informal — which? (está becomes estás, and usted becomes tú.) What does de nada literally say? ("Of nothing.") And if the person answering you says vos instead of tú — do you switch? (No. You understand it and keep saying tú.) Next chapter: farewells — hasta luego, hasta mañana, adiós.
